\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{लाजाः} (lājāḥ)}{लाजाः (lājāḥ)}]{\sk{लाजाः} (lājāḥ) — puffed rice}

\label{lesson:SA-C246-lajah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a clove, then the Sanskrit for cardamom.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{लाजाः}}
\textbf{\sk{लाजाः}} — \emph{lājāḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}puffed rice\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lājāḥ} is the plural of \emph{lāja}, \textquotedblleft{}fried or parched grain\textquotedblright{}, used in the plural for the grains (MW). MW files it under a root √lāj, \textquotedblleft{}to fry\textquotedblright{}, and it is already in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (CDIAL 11011). It lives on as Hindi \emph{lāī}, \textquotedblleft{}parched grain\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lājāḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{lājāḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a clove, then the Sanskrit for cardamom, then say \emph{lājāḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{धान्यम्} (dhānyam)}{धान्यम् (dhānyam)}]{\sk{धान्यम्} (dhānyam) — grain}

\label{lesson:SA-C246-dhanyam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for cardamom, then the Sanskrit for puffed rice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{धान्यम्}}
\textbf{\sk{धान्यम्}} — \emph{dhānyam} — \textquotedblleft{}grain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dhānya} means \textquotedblleft{}of grain\textquotedblright{}, and then \textquotedblleft{}grain, corn\textquotedblright{} itself; it is built on \emph{dhānā}, \textquotedblleft{}grain\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 6778). It lives on as Hindi \emph{dhān}, \textquotedblleft{}growing or unhusked rice\textquotedblright{}. It is a different word from \emph{dhanya}, \textquotedblleft{}fortunate\textquotedblright{}, in \emph{dhanyavādaḥ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{सक्तुः} (saktuḥ)}{सक्तुः (saktuḥ)}]{\sk{सक्तुः} (saktuḥ) — barley flour}

\label{lesson:SA-C246-saktuh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for puffed rice, then the Sanskrit for grain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सक्तुः}}
\textbf{\sk{सक्तुः}} — \emph{saktuḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}barley flour\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{saktu} is coarsely ground meal, especially of barley, already in the Rigveda (CDIAL 13070). MW gives no derivation, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{sattū}, the flour of parched grain.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{क्षौद्रम्} (kṣaudram)}{क्षौद्रम् (kṣaudram)}]{\sk{क्षौद्रम्} (kṣaudram) — wild honey}

\label{lesson:SA-C246-ksaudram}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for grain, then the Sanskrit for barley flour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{क्षौद्रम्}}
\textbf{\sk{क्षौद्रम्}} — \emph{kṣaudram} — \textquotedblleft{}wild honey\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kṣaudra} is built on \emph{kṣudrā}, \textquotedblleft{}a kind of bee\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{kṣudra}, \textquotedblleft{}tiny\textquotedblright{} (MW): the honey of small wild bees. MW glosses \emph{kṣaudra} \textquotedblleft{}honey, a species of honey\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{मिष्टान्नम्} (miṣṭānnam)}{मिष्टान्नम् (miṣṭānnam)}]{\sk{मिष्टान्नम्} (miṣṭānnam) — a sweet dish}

\label{lesson:SA-C246-mistannam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for barley flour, then the Sanskrit for wild honey.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मिष्टान्नम्}}
\textbf{\sk{मिष्टान्नम्}} — \emph{miṣṭānnam} — \textquotedblleft{}a sweet dish\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{miṣṭānna} is a compound of \emph{miṣṭa}, \textquotedblleft{}dainty, sweet\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{anna}, \textquotedblleft{}food\textquotedblright{} (MW), which you have already met. CDIAL 10299 lists \emph{miṣṭa} beside \emph{mṛṣṭa}, \textquotedblleft{}rubbed, prepared\textquotedblright{}, and Hindi \emph{mīṭhā}, \textquotedblleft{}sweet\textquotedblright{}, comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}
